result:
There is a light left on in almost every town that never goes out.

It's not the streetlight on Main, or the red eye of the radio tower blinking against the hills. It's smaller than that. It's the light above the stove in a diner that closed three hours ago. The one in the back hallway of the library. The one in your parents' house that they leave on over the sink, just in case you come home. Someone is paying a few cents an hour to keep a little circle of yellow going when no one is there to see it. I think about those lights a lot.

I think about maintenance. Not in the grand, world-changing sense, but in the literal sense: the act of maintaining. Someone has to keep the ice rink frozen in summer so it will be ready in winter. Someone has to tighten the bolts on the playground swing set before the chains get too thin. Someone has to wipe down the handrails at the airport. The world does not stay world-shaped on its own. Gravity would do its job, but everything else would slowly, politely fall apart.

If you ever work a closing shift anywhere, you know this. The real work starts after the customer leaves. At the bookstore where I would spend my afternoons when I was younger, the owner, Mrs. Jensen, would let me sit in the history aisle while she did what she called "putting the store to bed." She would straighten every book so its spine was exactly flush with the shelf edge. She would fluff the armchair cushions. She would water the drooping pothos plant that lived by the cash register. "Books don't sell themselves," she told me once, but that wasn't quite it. She wasn't selling them at 10:15 p.m. She was just reminding them that they mattered.

That's what I love about people. You are the only species we know of that will straighten a room that no one will see.

We have this strange habit of making museums for things. The big museums are obvious: fossils, paintings, wars. But we also make tiny, private museums that we don't call museums. Your junk drawer is a museum. Think about it. There's the takeout menu from the place that closed in 2019 that you can't throw away, the single IKEA Allen wrench, three dead pens, a birthday candle shaped like a 7, a stone you picked up on a beach because it looked like a heart and then you forgot why you kept it. It's curated by accident. It's an archive of almosts. Every drawer in every kitchen in the world is a small argument against entropy. "I might need this. This meant something once. I should keep it just in case."

We are all archivists of our own lives, and terrible at it. We remember the wrong things. We forget the name of the person we sat next to in math class for a year, but we remember exactly how the sun looked hitting the linoleum floor that one afternoon in October when we were nine and we were home sick. We remember that the grocery store used to have those little wax juice bottles. We remember the jingle for a commercial that hasn't aired in twenty years. Our brains are not filing cabinets. They are attics. Things get piled, and the important stuff ends up under a winter coat.

Sometimes I wonder what the Earth would look like if you could see all the lost pockets. Every couch cushion lifted up, exhaling a cloud of coins, crumbs, remote controls, Lego heads, hair ties, grocery receipts faded to white. Every street drain opening and showing the last ten years of dropped keys and earrings and bottle caps. Every pocket turned inside-out at once. It would be a brief, glittering snowstorm of small human things, and then it would settle, and we'd all bend down and say, "Oh, there it is. I was looking for that."

There is a theory, not a scientific one, just one I hold because it makes the day feel softer: that objects remember being held. Not in a mystical way. But that a coffee mug gets a little warmer faster in the hands that use it every morning. That a pair of shoes breaks in not just to a foot shape, but to a walk. The way your father opens a jar is different from how your friend opens a jar, and the lid somehow knows. We leave traces in the things we touch, even if no instrument can measure it. Use polishes the world.

My favorite time of day has always been the hour that doesn't belong to anyone. Not morning, not night. Around 5:30 a.m. in the summer. The sky is not dark and not light yet. It's that flat, washed-blue color, like denim left in the sun. The air is cool in a way it won't be by nine. In that hour, delivery trucks are the only cars on the road. Newspaper routes still exist somewhere, I hope. A dog barks once and then decides not to. Sprinklers start up on lawns with a rhythmic tick, tick, tick. If you're awake then, you feel like you are seeing the set before the play starts — the stagehands still moving chairs, the lights being tested, someone coughing in the wings.

You might think that nothing happens then, but everything is about to happen then. That is the whole point. It's the world inhaling.

We talk so much about big moments, but I think most of a life is lived in the intermissions. Waiting for the water to boil. Waiting for the crosswalk light to change. Standing in line at the pharmacy while your nose itches. Sitting in a parked car for an extra minute because the song hasn't ended yet. Those are not the empty spaces between life. Those *are* life. If you added up all the minutes you spent waiting for toast to pop, you would get weeks. Weeks of your life just standing there, watching the red coils. What did you think about while you waited? That's who you are.

If I could tell you one thing without it sounding like a poster in a guidance counselor's office, it would be this: pay attention to what you pay attention to when no one is asking you to pay attention to anything. When you're bored, what does your mind drift to? Do you replay arguments? Do you plan vacations you will never take? Do you count ceiling tiles? Do you think about how ants find their way back home? Your boredom is a very honest autobiography.

Here's another thing I think is true: we underestimate how much of our lives is already post-apocalyptic, in the best sense. Your favorite sweater has a hole in the elbow. You wear it anyway. Your car has 180,000 miles and a weird rattle when you turn left. You know how to ignore it. Your knees make a sound. Your apartment plant has lost three leaves but is still trying out a new one. We are all living in the after — after the newness. And we keep loving things anyway. We patch them. We tape them. We call them "perfectly good." That is not settling. That is grace.

The world will tell you a hundred times a day to want the next thing. The next phone, the next job title, the next version of yourself that is finally disciplined and drinks enough water. But the quietest and most persistent rebellion you can manage is to keep taking care of the old thing. To darn the sock. To reread the book. To call your mom not because it's a special occasion but because it's Tuesday.

If you have a light you leave on, leave it on. If you have a drawer full of almosts, keep it. If you have a morning hour that belongs to no one, sit in it for a minute. The universe is vast and expanding and mostly hydrogen, and somewhere in it, on a small rock with an unreliable magnetic field, someone is straightening chairs in an empty room because it matters that they are straight.

That is enough.
